items: Potential confounding from climate and environmental gradients: key climate variables were removed when collinear with yield/suitability, risking attribution of climate-driven biodiversity patterns to yield.

Space-for-time substitution and reliance on observational associations limit causal interpretation; intensification is proxied by yield, which itself reflects multiple, heterogeneous management pathways.
Potential spatial autocorrelation in residuals is not explicitly modeled (e.g., spatial random effects or autocovariates), which can bias standard errors and effect sizes.
Stepwise model selection via likelihood-ratio tests can inflate Type I error and yields unstable model structures relative to information-criterion or regularization-based approaches.
No explicit out-of-sample validation or predictive performance metrics to assess generalizability.

The expansion scenario assumes direct replacement of primary vegetation within already cultivated landscapes and linear biodiversity responses, omitting fragmentation and edge effects that can amplify losses.
RCAR relies on GBIF-derived range sizes that may be biased by uneven sampling effort; bias corrections or alternative range sources are not explored beyond citing prior robustness.
Uncertainty propagation in scenario projections (e.g., parametric and data-layer uncertainty) is not quantified.
The rationale and implications of weighting by crop area fraction could be discussed more transparently (e.g., potential biases if sampling within “cropland” is not the focal crop).
The interpretation of RCAR changes could be clarified with examples and cross-checks against community similarity metrics to aid reader intuition.
More explicit guidance on the magnitude and spatial distribution of effects (e.g., maps with confidence intervals, partial dependence plots) would improve interpretability.

The study could more explicitly situate its findings relative to integrated bioeconomic and land-use models showing rebound/compensatory dynamics and demand-side leverage (e.g., Leclère et al. 2020; related systems modeling and ABM work).

Recent work on ecological intensification and landscape configuration (hedgerows/SNH connectivity) and their scale-dependent effects on biodiversity and services could be more directly connected to managerial implications.

Potential confounding by range size and habitat amount: range area is a strong predictor of extinction risk yet appears absent from the model; the included “proportion suitable” may not adequately control for total range extent.

The fragmentation metric (mean interior distance to edge) is strongly correlated with habitat amount and patch size; although “proportion suitable” and “patch isolation” are included, residual collinearity and scale dependence could bias variable importance.

Temporal alignment is unclear: fragmentation appears to be measured at a single or limited time slice while extinction risk transitions span 1996–2020; HFP baselines (2000/2018) and IUCN dates (1996/2020) are misaligned, risking attribution biases.

The claim that fragmentation outperforms habitat loss is insufficiently supported because direct measures of habitat loss (e.g., AOH/land-cover loss over time) do not appear as predictors; changes in HFP within suitable habitat are not equivalent to habitat loss.

The binary split of matrix quality at 50% high-HFP is arbitrary; although an interaction is modeled continuously (Fig. 3), robustness to other splits/thresholds (e.g., HFP ≥1, 4, 7, 10) is not assessed.
Unaddressed spatial and phylogenetic autocorrelation may inflate model performance and importance metrics; cross-validation that does not block by realm/region or phylogeny can overstate generality.
IUCN category changes can be non-genuine (taxonomy/knowledge/criteria revisions). There is no indication that these were filtered or modeled, which may contaminate the signal.

Methods detail for key computations (e.g., exact fragmentation computation, spatial resolution, weighting across patches, time points used for fragmentation/HFP) is insufficient in the excerpt; reproducibility would benefit from more explicit descriptions and code availability.
The choice and calculation of variable-importance metric (e.g., permutation vs Gini) and steps to mitigate bias from correlated predictors are not stated.

Climate change exposure (e.g., thermal stress variability, climate velocity) is not incorporated, despite its growing role in extinction risk; comparison to studies emphasizing climatic drivers would contextualize scope.
Alternative connectivity/fragmentation measures (graph-theoretic connectivity, resistance-based metrics using HFP or land cover, effective mesh size) are not discussed or tested.

No comparison with other recent extinction-risk modeling pipelines that integrate SDMs, land-use change, and human pressures (e.g., deep-SDM-based risk classifiers) to benchmark predictive power and interpretability.

Lack of detail on critical FL choices (e.g., exact aggregation weighting, straggler handling, participation variability per round) given severe client-size imbalance raises concerns about convergence dynamics and representation equity across sites.

Model design uses three independent sigmoid channels for nested labels (ET ⊂ TC ⊂ WT) without explicit structural constraints; potential inconsistencies and missed opportunities for topology-aware learning are not addressed.

Privacy is improved via TEE on the aggregator, but there is no analysis of client update leakage risk (e.g., gradient inversion, membership inference) or use of secure aggregation/differential privacy.

Comparisons are limited to the “public initial model”; there is no strong baseline such as (i) centralized training on any sizable shareable subset, (ii) state-of-the-art backbones (e.g., nnU-Net) retrained under comparable constraints, or (iii) alternative FL algorithms (e.g., FedProx, personalized FL, or DG-enhanced FL).
Reporting relies primarily on DSC; boundary metrics (e.g., HD95, surface Dice) important for surgical/radiation planning are missing.
The p-value reported for the quantized model’s “insignificant” drop (pAverage < 7 × 10^-5) contradicts the textual claim; effect sizes and confidence intervals are not provided.

Ambiguity about annotation provenance and quality control: the methods mention label fusion and integration with multiple algorithms, but it is unclear when/where automated labels were used, how manual refinements were standardized, and whether inter-rater reliability was assessed across 71 sites.

Preprocessing details (e.g., intensity normalization, resampling strategy for 2D/3D, skull stripping failure handling) are not sufficiently specified to ensure reproducibility and to interpret domain-shift mitigation.

Limited discussion of modern FL/DG approaches that explicitly tackle domain heterogeneity (e.g., domain-specific normalization, style mixing, hierarchical aggregation, augmentation-based DG in FL). Positioning against recent methods (e.g., TreeFedDG, augmentation-driven FL/DG, style-based DG) is missing.
No analysis of fairness or subgroup performance (e.g., per site/continent, scanner vendor, sex/age), despite claims about enabling underrepresented populations.
